title: How did The Beatles get their name?

entries.note: First used of ships rocking and rolling at sea, then in African-American slang and as a sexual euphemism; the OED spells it rock 'n' roll; popularised by [[see:Alan Freed]].
A traditional folk song sung by a retired Welsh seaman, which uses [[see:rock and roll]] as a sexual euphemism.
A DJ credited with taking the music to white audiences in the 1950s by calling it [[see:rock and roll]].
Said to have been coined by Billboard magazine as a euphemism replacing [[see:race records]] for music of Black origin.
Music industry term, also race music, for records marketed to African-American audiences from the 1920s to the 1940s; contrasted with [[see:hillbilly records]].
Industry term, also hillbilly music, for bluegrass-style music marketed to white audiences in the South, which turned into [[gave:country music]].
The genre that [[from:hillbilly records]] turned into.
From [[from:blue devils]], meaning sadness by the 1700s; became the genre's name after song titles like Memphis Blues; first musical use in [[see:Charlotte Forten Grimké]]'s diary.
A 1600s term for harmful spirits, hallucinations and mental anguish, later used for despair by Jefferson and Byron; gave [[gave:the blues]].
A free Black teacher from Pennsylvania whose Civil War diary contains the first printed musical use of [[see:the blues]].
African-American term for an informal venue for music, dancing and gambling, where blues and rock and roll spread; probably from a Gullah word meaning rowdy.
Takes its name from the [[from:juke joint]].

A pun blending beetles and beat, coined by John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe, inspired by [[see:The Crickets]]; earlier names included [[see:The Quarrymen]] and [[see:Long John and the Silver Beatles]].
Buddy Holly's band, which John Lennon cited as the insect-name inspiration for [[see:The Beatles]].

entries.term: Long John and the Silver Beatles
entries.note: Name suggested by [[see:Casey Jones]] because The Beatles had too few syllables; John Lennon sometimes went by Long John; later shortened to [[see:The Silver Beatles]].
Shortened from [[from:Long John and the Silver Beatles]] before the band became simply [[see:The Beatles]].
Stage name Paul McCartney used in the early days of [[see:The Beatles]].
[[see:Casey Jones]]'s band, more successful than The Beatles at the time.
Stage name of Brian Cassar, who advised The Beatles; apparently borrowed from [[from?:The Ballad of Casey Jones]].
The ballad Jess suggests [[see:Casey Jones]] took his stage name from.
A legendary blues club in Chicago, pictured on Jess's t-shirt.
One of the earlier names of [[see:The Beatles]].
Another early name of [[see:The Beatles]].
Originally [[see:The Ravens]]; the name was a gimmick alluding to kinkiness, meant to be subversive and attract publicity.
The original name of [[see:The Kinks]], one of many animal band names of the time.
An announcer forgot their ever-changing name and used their song title Butthole Surfer; some TV and radio stations refused to say it.
Named after a dildo, Steely Dan III from Yokohama, in [[from:Naked Lunch]] by William S. Burroughs; the book says it's rubber, not steam-powered.
William S. Burroughs's 1959 novel, the subject of a landmark US obscenity case and the source of [[see:Steely Dan]].
Supposedly named for the average amount of a man's ejaculation.
From the remark that Jimmy Page's supergroup would [[from:go down like a lead balloon]]; respelled so it wouldn't be read as 'leed'.

entries.term: go down like a lead balloon
entries.note: Said of the planned supergroup, perhaps by Keith Moon; Jess confirms the phrase is known in the US; gave [[gave:Led Zeppelin]].
Originally Deaf Leopard, from a Sheffield school art lesson; respelled in a way that echoes [[see:Led Zeppelin]], preferring that to sounding like [[see:The Flying Lizards]].
Band [[see:Def Leppard]] said they'd rather not resemble, because its name just describes an odd animal.
A deliberate misspelling of the name of [[from:Leonard Skinner]], and supposedly still pronounced like it.
The gym teacher at the band's school after whom [[see:Lynyrd Skynyrd]] are named.
Rob's instrument, also called a banjolele, bought on eBay from [[see:Survivor Guitars]].
Guitar shop set up by a [[see:Lynyrd Skynyrd]] roadie who survived the band's air crash; spelled Syrvyvr, with Ys replacing the vowels.
Decorative umlauts in band names, as in [[see:Mötley Crüe]] and [[see:Motörhead]], making a name look Germanic and dark and marking membership of the fraternity.
Example of the [[see:metal umlaut]]; the band were surprised when German fans pronounced the umlauts.
Example of the [[see:metal umlaut]].
Another band name with a [[see:metal umlaut]].
A band with an unexplained umlaut over the i, an example of the [[see:metal umlaut]].
Puts a [[see:metal umlaut]] over the n, a letter that can't normally take one.
An American industrial rock band with a [[see:metal umlaut]] over every consonant in its name.
Formerly [[see:Spice]]; named after the sycophantic David Copperfield villain in Dickens's centenary year; debut album referenced his 'very 'umble' line.
The original name of [[see:Uriah Heep]].
From a passage about 'modest mouse colored people' in Virginia Woolf's story [[from:The Mark on the Wall]].
Formerly [[see:El Grupo de Rock and Roll]]; named after a film and play whose judge imagines himself Sherlock Holmes, alluding to Don Quixote's windmills.

entries.term: El Grupo de Rock and Roll
entries.note: The original name of [[see:They Might Be Giants]], which Rob prefers.
Named after Aldous Huxley's essay [[from:The Doors of Perception]].
Aldous Huxley's essay written after taking mescaline, titled from a William Blake quotation; gave [[gave:The Doors]].
First suggested by a psychiatrist in a letter to Aldous Huxley about their mescaline experiments.
Named after a disapproving 1963 non-fiction exposé on swinging, orgies and BDSM, later appropriated by queer culture.
Named after [[from:Greenwich Village]]; made for the gay disco market, with members modelled on macho archetypes ('must dance and have a mustache').
New York neighbourhood, site of the Stonewall Uprising and birthplace of the modern LGBTQ rights movement, which gave [[gave:Village People]] their name.
[[see:Village People]] song once considered by the Navy; a founding member recently denied it is a gay anthem.
Named after a Boris Karloff horror film showing across the street, as people pay to see horror; formerly the [[see:Polka Tulk Blues Band]].
One of the lame earlier names of [[see:Black Sabbath]].
A band name with a classical reference that Jess thinks goes harder than its music.
From Sanskrit, meaning to blow away or wipe out; the Buddhist release from self, karma and the cycle of rebirth.
A genre named by people who didn't like it, like [[see:punk]].
A word meaning horrible or inferior, applied to the music and then adopted by musicians who liked its rawness.
From Philip Horky's 1997 poetry collection Child's Reflections, Cold Play; earlier names were [[see:Big Fat Noises]] and [[see:Starfish]], plus the joke name Pectoralz.
An early name of [[see:Coldplay]].
Another early name of [[see:Coldplay]].
Originally known as Naked Toddler.
Formerly Darlin', after a Beach Boys single; renamed after a Melody Maker review called their music 'a daft punky thrash'.
German hip-hop band named after a fan's praise; fett meant great and Brot was slang for hash, so 'really good hash'.
Chosen because the band were very into industry.
A German band whose name means the doctors.
Popular German band named from the idiom [[from:tote Hose]].
German idiom for having nothing going on, being bored or time-wasting; gave [[gave:Die Toten Hosen]].
Named after their own song about the air show disaster at [[from:Ramstein]]; the extra M came from misspelling it on their equipment.
A US air base in Germany where an air show crash killed about 70 people, giving [[gave:Rammstein]] their name.
The singer's name is Icelandic for birch.
Also the name, written as one word, of the lead singer's sister, born as the band started.
Eurovision-winning Italian band whose Danish name was suggested by their half-Danish bassist.
The duo who sang the Macarena.
The band that recorded La Bamba.
The Korean band say in English that it stands for 'beyond the scene', but the initialism comes from Korean for bulletproof boy scouts.
A Taylor Swift lyric that became a meme; Jess picked it up without realising where it came from.
Belgian singer whose name is the [[see:verlan]] form of [[from:maestro]], with the two syllables swapped.
A long-standing form of French back slang that swaps the sounds of words, as in [[see:Stromae]], [[see:meuf]] and [[see:cimer]].
The word reversed to make [[see:Stromae]].
Young French people's word for a woman, the [[see:verlan]] form of femme.
The [[see:verlan]] form of bizarre.
A greeting, the [[see:verlan]] form of bonjour.
The [[see:verlan]] form of français.
The [[see:verlan]] form of merci, used to say thanks.
French artist whose album [[see:Laisse béton]] Rob discovered uses [[see:verlan]].
Album by [[see:Renaud]]; Rob thought it meant leave concrete, but it is the [[see:verlan]] form of [[from:laisse tomber]].
French for let it go or just leave it; reversed in [[see:verlan]] to give [[gave:Laisse béton]].
